title: Complete Blood Count Interpretation
subject: Medicine
summary: A complete blood count (CBC) gives a rapid snapshot of the cellular components of blood. Interpreting the numbers helps clinicians locate infection, inflammation, bleeding, marrow failure or chronic disease, especially where advanced imaging is scarce.

sections.p: The CBC measures red cells, white cells (with differential), and platelets using an automated analyser. It is the first laboratory test for any undifferentiated sick patient.
b: Haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV assess anaemia type.
Total WBC and differential identify infection, inflammation or marrow stress.
Platelet count screens for bleeding risk and marrow suppression.

sections.p: Severity is judged by how far values deviate from normal ranges and by clinical impact (e.g., haemoglobin <7 g/dL = severe anaemia needing transfusion).
b: Mild anaemia: Hb 10‑12 g/dL (women) or 11‑13 g/dL (men).
Moderate anaemia: Hb 7‑9 g/dL.
Severe anaemia: Hb <7 g/dL.
Leukocytosis: WBC >11 ×10⁹/L; leukopenia: <4 ×10⁹/L.
Thrombocytopenia: platelets <100 ×10⁹/L; severe <50 ×10⁹/L.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common drivers of abnormal CBCs are infections (malaria, HIV, TB, bacterial sepsis), nutritional deficiencies, sickle‑cell disease and chronic haemolysis.
b: Anaemia – malaria, hookworm, iron deficiency, sickle‑cell, chronic kidney disease.
Leukocytosis – bacterial sepsis, malaria, TB, HIV opportunistic infection.
Leukopenia – advanced HIV, severe malaria, aplastic crisis in sickle‑cell.
Thrombocytopenia – malaria, dengue, HIV, drug‑induced marrow suppression.

sections.p: Patients may present with fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea (anaemia), fever, chills, rigors (leukocytosis), bruising or bleeding (thrombocytopenia). In malaria the CBC often shows anaemia with thrombocytopenia and a left‑shifted neutrophil count.
b: Anaemia → tachycardia, orthostatic dizziness, conjunctival pallor.
Leukocytosis → fever, rigors, focal pain.
Thrombocytopenia → petechiae, mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts.

sections.p: The CBC is the backbone; additional tests are guided by the pattern of abnormality.

t.b: What cell morphology is present? → Detect malaria parasites, sickle cells, schistocytes, blasts.
Is the marrow responding? → High in haemolysis or blood loss; low in iron deficiency or marrow failure.
Is iron deficiency the cause of microcytic anaemia? → Low ferritin confirms deficiency.
Is HIV contributing to cytopenias? → Positive test prompts ART and opportunistic infection work‑up.
Is there marrow infiltration or aplasia? → Needed when pancytopenia persists without clear peripheral cause.
What to do? → Use rapid malaria antigen test; consider empirical antimalarial if clinical picture fits.

sections.p: Certain CBC patterns herald life‑threatening states that need urgent action.
b: Hb <7 g/dL with cardiac failure → risk of sudden decompensation.
WBC >25 ×10⁹/L with left shift → possible sepsis or leukemoid reaction.
Platelets <20 ×10⁹/L → spontaneous intracranial bleed risk.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then correct the specific cytopenia if it threatens organ function.
b: Anaemia – treat malaria, give iron/folate, transfuse if Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic.
Leukocytosis – start empiric antibiotics for sepsis; add antimalarial if smear positive.
Leukopenia in HIV – start ART, consider prophylactic cotrimoxazole.
Thrombocytopenia – stop offending drugs, treat malaria, give platelet transfusion if <20 ×10⁹/L with bleeding.

sections.p: Repeat CBC after 48‑72 h of therapy to gauge response. Prevent recurrence with vector control, deworming, iron supplementation programs and HIV screening.
b: Re‑check Hb after malaria treatment; expect rise of 1‑2 g/dL per week.
Monitor WBC trend; falling count suggests effective infection control.
Educate patients on avoiding herbal remedies that cause marrow suppression.
Anaemia of chronic disease vs iron‑deficiency – differentiate with ferritin and CRP.
Leukocytosis from stress vs bacterial infection – look for left shift and clinical sepsis signs.
Thrombocytopenia from malaria vs dengue – dengue often has marked leukopenia and high transaminases.
Hemolysis in sample can falsely raise potassium and lower haemoglobin.
Cold agglutinins can cause spuriously low platelet counts on automated analysers.
Severe dehydration concentrates cells, giving a pseudo‑leukocytosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL) with chest pain or syncope

faq.q: Why does malaria cause low platelets?
faq.a: Parasite‑induced splenic sequestration and immune‑mediated destruction lower platelet counts.

faq.q: Can a normal CBC rule out serious infection?
faq.a: No; early sepsis may have normal WBC, so rely on clinical picture and other labs like CRP.

faq.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated for anaemia?
faq.a: When Hb <7 g/dL or <9 g/dL with cardiac disease, severe symptoms, or active bleeding.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with fever and a CBC showing Hb 6 g/dL, WBC 15 ×10⁹/L, platelets 120 ×10⁹/L — discuss immediate priorities and why transfusion may be needed.
A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 10 µg/L — explain the diagnostic steps to confirm iron‑deficiency anaemia and rule out anaemia of chronic disease.
A patient with confirmed malaria has Hb 8 g/dL, platelets 45 ×10⁹/L, WBC 5 ×10⁹/L — what supportive measures are essential and how does malaria explain the platelet count?

You receive a CBC with WBC 30 ×10⁹/L, neutrophils 85 % and left‑shifted bands, but the patient is afebrile and looks well — what differential diagnoses should you consider and what next test would you order?
A pregnant woman in a rural clinic has Hb 10 g/dL, MCV 85 fL, platelets 150 ×10⁹/L — what are the main causes of her mild anaemia and how would you manage it without iron studies?
A patient on long‑term methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis shows platelets 80 ×10⁹/L and WBC 3 ×10⁹/L — why must the drug be stopped and what alternative therapy is safer in low‑resource settings?
A child with severe malnutrition presents with Hb 5 g/dL, reticulocyte count 0.5 % — interpret the marrow response and outline the next steps in management.
